content.title: About
content.content: Watercress (Nasturtium officinale) is a fast‑growing aquatic leafy plant widely used in cooking. When cooked it retains a mildly peppery flavor and a pleasant crunch, making it a popular addition to soups, stews, omelets and side dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Watercress grows in clean, flowing freshwater and is an indicator of water quality.
It contains 5‑6 times more vitamin C than an orange per gram of fresh weight.
Ancient Romans used it as a remedy for colds and to aid digestion.
Watercress belongs to the cruciferous family, alongside broccoli and cabbage.
Heat treatment reduces some of its bitterness while softening the aroma.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C boosts immunity and is essential for collagen synthesis, supporting skin and blood‑vessel health.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Beta‑carotene, lutein and zeaxanthin in watercress protect cells from oxidative damage.

items.title: Supports bone health
items.content: Calcium and vitamin K help maintain strong bones and proper blood clotting.

items.title: Low‑calorie protein source
items.content: Cooked watercress retains a modest amount of plant protein, useful for vegetarian diets.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: Fiber and bitter compounds stimulate bile production, improving fat digestion.

items.title: Water contamination
items.content: The plant can accumulate bacteria and heavy metals from polluted water; thorough washing and cooking are recommended.

items.title: Thyroid interaction
items.content: Glucosinolates may affect thyroid function if consumed in very large amounts.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: A small number of people may experience an allergy to cruciferous vegetables.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Watercress is typically blanched for 1‑2 minutes, then quickly sautéed or added at the end of cooking to preserve its bright color and flavor. It works well in soups, pasta, omelets, and as a garnish for meat or fish dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh watercress in the refrigerator in a sealed container lined with a damp paper towel, and use within 3‑4 days. Cooked watercress should be stored in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 2 days.
